description: CT-RATE is a public dataset comprising 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans (50,188 reconstructed volumes, over 14.3 million 2D slices) from 21,304 unique patients, each paired with a corresponding radiology report. Each CT exam is accompanied by a report including impression and findings sections authored by a radiologist, and each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities. The dataset is fully open-source and designed to support development of foundation models for 3D medical imaging.
name: CT-RATE
publisher: Istanbul Medipol University / University of Zurich
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each CT volume is annotated with 18 abnormality labels. Radiology reports (one per CT exam) were authored by radiologists as part of clinical practice.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Radiology reports were authored by numerous radiologists at Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital (reflecting a variety of writing styles). Report translations were reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students. Expert evaluation of CT-CHAT outputs was performed by three board-certified radiologists: two thoracic radiologists from Zurich (R1, R2) and one from Istanbul (R3).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The finetuned text encoder (RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m) for automatic label extraction was evaluated on a 200-report validation set. Precision, recall, and F1 scores were computed per abnormality, showing robust classification: most abnormalities achieved F1 scores of 0.95–1.00 (e.g., Pericardial effusion F1=1.00, Pleural effusion F1=1.00, Interlobular septal thickening F1=1.00; lowest was Bronchiectasis at F1=0.95).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Manual annotation was performed in-house (no external crowdsourcing platform mentioned). Automated label extraction used a finetuned RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Multi-abnormality labels were extracted from radiology reports using an automated text classifier. First, 1,000 reports were manually annotated for 18 distinct abnormalities by merging findings and impression sections. Conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent. Similar conditions were grouped (e.g., left and right mucoid impactions under 'mucoid impaction'; lung opacity, density increase, and ground-glass opacities under 'lung opacity'; lung and fissural nodules as 'lung nodules'). The annotated reports were divided into training (80%, 800 reports) and validation (20%, 200 reports) sets. A pretrained language model (RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m) was then finetuned on these 1,000 manually annotated reports and applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports.
rai:dataBiases: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (1) CT-RATE is a single-institution dataset from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital in Türkiye, which may introduce geographic and clinical setting biases that limit generalizability to other populations. (2) CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection; variability in how diseases are described across radiology reports can affect detection accuracy. (3) The dataset reflects real-world heterogeneity (diverse scanners, acquisition protocols, reconstruction techniques) rather than a curated study dataset, which is considered a design strength for robustness.
rai:dataCollection: CT-RATE was curated from chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. The dataset includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023, totaling 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. The cohort was divided into 20,000 patients for training and 1,304 for validation. CT volumes were reconstructed using various techniques (different kernels) to suit different window settings. Patients range in age from 18 to 102 years (mean 48.8, mode 40). Sex distribution is 41.6% female and 58.4% male. Scanners used: 61.5% Philips, 30.1% Siemens, 8.4% PNMS.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes in various resolutions (65.4% in 512×512 px, 4.2% in 768×768 px, 30.4% in 1024×1024 px), with pixel spacing in the axial (XY) plane ranging from 0.227 to 1.416 mm (mean 0.605 mm), slice thickness ranging from 0.035 to 6 mm (mean 1.231 mm), and number of slices per volume ranging from 100 to 600 (average 304.7). Radiology reports are structured into four sections: clinical information, technique, findings, and impression, originally written in Turkish by radiologists.
rai:dataLimitations: 1) Single-institution dataset from one geographic and clinical setting, limiting generalizability to other populations. 2) CT-CLIP depends on specific terminology in reports and prompt choice for zero-shot detection. 3) Current models are limited to chest CT volumes; other 3D imaging modalities (MRI, PET) and anatomical regions are not covered. 4) Abnormality detection performance still falls short of clinical deployment thresholds. 5) The quality of generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use. 6) Detailed metadata for the second external validation set (UPMC) is not publicly available as it is a private dataset.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Every reconstructed volume from the hospital database was incorporated (including different reconstruction kernels for different window settings). The dataset was split into training (20,000 patients) and internal validation (1,304 patients) sets. For CT-CHAT training, a VQA dataset of over 2.7 million question-answer pairs was derived from CT-RATE reports using Llama 3.1 8B. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using TotalSegmentator and included in the repository. Nodule segmentation information (lobar location, centroid, diameters, volumes) was extracted using a 3D nodule segmentation algorithm for CT-CHAT report generation enhancement.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: 1) Reports were anonymized by removing personal information using regular expressions to identify and eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers. 2) Anonymized reports were translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API, reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students. 3) CT volumes were quality-controlled: volumes involving contrast material or body parts other than the chest were excluded. 4) Each CT volume's orientation was standardized by examining its metadata. 5) All identifying information was removed from metadata. 6) For model training, volumes were resized to uniform spacing of 0.75 mm (x-axis and y-axis) and 1.5 mm (z-axis), then center-cropped or padded to 480×480×240 resolution. 7) CT volumes were converted to Hounsfield Unit (HU) values using intercept and slope from metadata, clipped to -1000 to 1000 HU. 8) During training, HU values were normalized to -1 to 1.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors plan to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work. As an initial step, organ-level anatomical segmentation labels generated using TotalSegmentator are openly available through the CT-RATE repository on Hugging Face.
rai:dataSocialImpact: CT-RATE addresses the scarcity of comprehensive 3D medical imaging datasets paired with textual reports, enabling development of AI foundation models for 3D medical imaging. The open-source release aims to reduce the workload on radiologists, potentially improve diagnostic accuracy, and support patient care in situations where immediate radiological expertise is not available. The authors note that substantial progress is still needed before clinical deployment, and challenges such as robustness, interpretability, regulatory compliance, and prospective validation must be addressed. Ethical approval was granted by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee at Istanbul Medipol University (E-10840098-772.02-6841, 27/10/2023) for open-sourcing the dataset.
rai:dataUseCases: Intended use cases include: (1) training contrastive language-image pretraining models for 3D chest CT (CT-CLIP); (2) multi-abnormality detection in chest CT volumes; (3) CT volume-to-volume retrieval; (4) report-to-volume retrieval; (5) training vision-language AI assistants for 3D chest CT (CT-CHAT); (6) visual question answering for chest CT; (7) radiology report generation; (8) anatomical localization and visual grounding using segmentation labels; (9) future multi-abnormality segmentation research.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m (finetuned on 1,000 manually annotated reports) was used to automatically extract 18 abnormality labels from the remaining 24,692 radiology reports. Google Translate API was used to translate reports from Turkish to English. TotalSegmentator was used to generate organ-level anatomical segmentation labels. Llama 3.1 8B was used to generate over 2.7 million VQA question-answer pairs for CT-CHAT training.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains medical imaging data (chest CT volumes) and radiology reports. All patient and medical professional identifying information was removed: reports were anonymized using regular expressions to eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers; CT volume metadata was anonymized by removing all identifying information about patients and medical professionals. Only anonymized metadata and English-translated reports are included in the open-sourced dataset.

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling in the collection process; volumes with contrast material or non-chest body parts were excluded (quality control), but no discussion of missing observations, incomplete records, or gaps in the collected data.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described for the dataset itself; padding of CT volumes to consistent resolution (480x480x240) is covered under preprocessing. Text token padding with PAD token is a model training detail, not a dataset imputation protocol.
